steps.body: |x| is almost always taught as “make it positive,” and that description survives exactly as long as the numbers stay simple. The honest definition is geometric: |x| is the DISTANCE from x to 0 on the number line. Distance has no direction, which is why it is never negative — not because a sign was deleted.
Place the marker and watch two different numbers describe it.

commonPlacements.feedback: That is −6's mirror image. Same distance from 0, opposite side — which is exactly the point: |6| and |−6| agree, 6 and −6 do not.
Too far left. Count six units from 0, not eight.

widget.prompt: Place the marker at −6. Watch the position readout and the distance readout.
widget.successFeedback: Position −6, distance 6. One marker, two honest numbers — and only the distance is |−6|.
widget.lowFeedback: Too far left — you have passed −6.
widget.highFeedback: Not far enough left — keep going toward −6.

predict.prompt: The marker will sit at −6. What will the two readouts say?

options.label: Both 6 — absolute value rewrites the position

predict.reveal: Position and distance are different questions about the same marker. Where is it? −6. How far from 0? 6. Absolute value answers only the second, which is why it never rewrites where the number actually lives.

explanationVariants: |−6| = 6 and |4| = 4, and 6 > 4, so −6 sits farther from zero even though −6 is the smaller number.
Distance ignores side: six units left beats four units right.

widget.prompt: Which number is FARTHER from 0: −6 or 4?

options.label: −6, because |−6| = 6
options.feedback: Yes — six units out beats four, and the side it went does not enter the comparison.

options.label: 4, because −6 is smaller than 4
options.feedback: That compares POSITION, not distance. −6 is indeed the smaller number, and still the farther one from zero.

options.label: They are equally far
options.feedback: Equal distance would need equal magnitudes: 6 ≠ 4.

steps.body: So two numbers can share a distance while disagreeing about everything else. |−6| = |6| = 6, but −6 ≠ 6. Absolute value throws away the side and keeps the size; the number itself is unharmed by being measured.

explanationVariants: |−9| asks how far −9 is from 0: nine units, so the value is 9.
Nine units left of zero is still nine units of distance — |−9| = 9.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the input, not its distance. −9 sits nine units from 0, so the distance is 9.
Zero would mean −9 sits ON zero. It sits nine units to the left.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count units from 0 to −9: nine of them. |−9| = 9.
widget.successFeedback: 9 — the distance, positive because distances are.

explanationVariants: |−7| = 7 and |5| = 5, so −7 is farther out despite being the smaller number.
Strip the signs to compare distances: 7 against 5.

widget.prompt: Which has the GREATER absolute value: −7 or 5?

options.feedback: Right: 7 > 5. The negative sign changed the side, never the size.
5 is the larger NUMBER, but |−7| = 7 > 5 = |5|. Bigger value, smaller distance.

options.label: Neither — absolute values are always equal
options.feedback: Absolute values differ whenever magnitudes differ; 7 ≠ 5.

explanationVariants: Two points sit exactly five units from 0: 5 and −5.
Distance five, either direction — so exactly two integers qualify.
hints: Draw the number line and mark every point exactly five units from 0.
Distance does not care about direction, so check the left side as well as the right.
5 is five units right of 0; −5 is five units left. Count them.

widget.prompt: How many different values of x satisfy |x| = 5?

commonErrors.feedback: Only if distance had a direction. Five units LEFT of zero works just as well as five units right.
That is the distance itself, not the number of solutions. Count the qualifying points: 5 and −5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Exactly two points lie five units from 0 — one on each side: x = 5 and x = −5.
widget.successFeedback: Two — and that pair is the whole reason absolute-value equations behave the way the next chapter shows.

takeaways: |x| is the distance from x to 0, which is why it is never negative.
Absolute value discards the side and keeps the size: |−6| = |6| = 6, but −6 ≠ 6.
Equal distances usually come in pairs — one on each side of zero.
steps.teaser: Next: plot |x| at every input and watch the pair-of-distances idea draw a V.
